nameStory: The red-throated loon gets its name from the stunning reddish throat patch that males and females both sport during breeding season. This crimson bib stands out dramatically against their otherwise gray and white plumage, making them unmistakable when they're dressed up for romance in spring and early summer.
description: The red-throated loon is the smallest member of the loon family, measuring about 22-26 inches long with a sleek, streamlined body built for diving. These aquatic birds are expert underwater hunters with dagger-like bills and legs positioned far back on their bodies for powerful swimming. In winter, they're fairly plain gray above and white below, but during breeding season they develop that famous red throat patch along with intricate black and white patterns on their backs.

idTips.label: Red throat patch
idTips.description: During breeding season, look for the distinctive rusty-red or brick-colored throat patch that gives this loon its name - it's triangular and unmistakable

idTips.label: Upward-tilted bill
idTips.description: The thin, dark bill often appears to tilt slightly upward, giving the bird a distinctive profile that's different from other loons

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than the more common Common Loon - about the size of a large duck rather than a small goose

idTips.label: Winter plumage
idTips.description: In winter, appears as a plain gray-backed bird with white underparts and a thin, straight neck - much more subdued than breeding colors

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with rapid wingbeats and neck extended straight forward, often calling with a distinctive kwuk-kwuk-kwuk sound

habitat: In New England, you'll spot red-throated loons along the coast during fall, winter, and early spring, especially in protected bays, harbors, and nearshore waters. They prefer areas with good fish populations and are often seen from rocky headlands, beaches, and piers. Unlike Common Loons, they rarely venture onto inland lakes during migration, sticking close to saltwater environments.

seasonality.spring: Look for birds transitioning into breeding plumage with developing red throat patches as they migrate north along the coast in April and May before heading to Arctic nesting grounds.
seasonality.summer: Rare in New England during summer as they've moved north to breed in Arctic regions, though occasional non-breeding individuals might be spotted along the coast.
seasonality.fall: Peak viewing time as birds migrate south in October and November, often still showing remnants of their breeding plumage before molting into winter colors.
seasonality.winter: Most easily found December through March in coastal waters, wearing their plain gray and white winter plumage while feeding in New England's ice-free bays and harbors.

funFact: Unlike other loons that need a long runway of water to take off, red-throated loons can actually take flight directly from land - they're the only loon species capable of this aerial feat, making them incredibly versatile in where they can nest and feed.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Common Loons, especially in winter when both lack distinctive markings. Remember 'smaller and simpler' - red-throated loons are noticeably smaller with a thinner neck and that slightly upturned bill, while Common Loons are bulkier with a perfectly straight, more robust bill.
contextualKnowledge: In Europe, this same species is called a 'red-throated diver' rather than a loon, reflecting different regional naming traditions for the same family of birds. The name 'loon' itself comes from their haunting calls, derived from Old Norse meaning 'to moan.'
compareHints: Red-throated loons are much smaller and more delicate-looking than Common Loons, with a thinner neck and that characteristic upward-tilted bill. While Common Loons have bold black and white checkerboard patterns in breeding plumage, red-throated loons keep things simpler with just that red throat patch and subtle back markings. In winter, size and bill shape remain your best clues for telling them apart.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common loons are much larger than red-throated loons, their only regular loon relative in New England waters.
Pacific Loons are the 'Goldilocks' of their family - not as large and blocky as Common Loons, not as small and delicate as Red-throated Loons, but just right in between.
Yellow-billed Loons dwarf their Common Loon cousins in size and have that unmistakable straight yellow bill versus the Common Loon's dark, slightly curved bill.
